claims.note: The fit passes exactly through the abstract's two end points (32.2/14.3 = 2.25 d at 23.9 °C; 32.2/3.2 = 10.1 d at 12.8 °C) but runs 9–14 % SHORT of the measured means in between: 2.67 vs 2.92 d at 21.7 °C, 2.80 vs 3.25 at 21.1, 3.27 vs 3.75 at 19.4, 3.69 vs 4.08 at 18.3, 5.41 vs 6.25 at 15.6, 5.96 vs 6.96 at 15.0 — the very 15–19 °C range the model's bass eggs develop in. A fit to all ten points (project computation): least squares on log D gives D ≈ 36.8/(T − 9.2) (residuals −9 % to +11 %); regression of 1/D on T gives D ≈ 33.6/(T − 9.9). Refit to the full table, or say the fit is to the two end points only. claims.note: If these share the comment's attribution to Webster 1948, he gives neither: his laboratory eggs developed 'without appreciable mortality' (no percentages), nothing was measured in nests, and swim-up timing is not reported (fry were kept only 'several days'). notes: The article's main finding, used by egg_stage.md: abrupt shifts of 50–75 °F (10–24 °C) at 0–4 days of incubation, and a rise of up to 24 °F just before hatch, did not kill eggs; no eggs were incubated successfully above 80 °F (fouling or temperature, not resolved); none were held below 50 °F. Field: 1945, eight early Taughannock Creek nests largely deserted when the water fell from 56 to slightly below 50 °F, yet the eggs were not killed; June 1946 mean daily fluctuation 10.5 ± 3.5 °F (extremes 52–80 °F). Fungus could envelop a whole nest within a day or so, with little relation to the male's presence. Literature incubation times (Table 1) run longer than his constant-temperature values, which he attributes to day–night fluctuation. For Table 3.6-1's '~4 d at 15.2–18.2 °C' (Turner & MacCrimmon 1970, not this key): Webster's constant-temperature eggs took 4.1 d at 18.3 °C but 6.3–7.0 d at 15.0–15.6 °C.
